name: Chapter 14: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
description: Respiratory organs, human respiratory system, breathing mechanism, lung volumes, gas exchange and transport, regulation, disorders

cards.definition: Exchange of O₂ from the atmosphere with CO₂ produced by cells; commonly called respiration
It is harmful (it forms acid and disturbs pH)

Sponges, coelenterates, flatworms: Diffusion over body surface; Earthworm: Moist cuticle; Insects: Tracheal tubes; Aquatic arthropods, molluscs, fishes: Gills (branchial); Terrestrial forms: amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals: Lungs (pulmonary); Frog (extra): Moist skin (cutaneous)

cards.term: On what does the breathing mechanism of an animal depend?
cards.definition: Its habitat and level of organisation
Respiration by gills
Respiration through moist skin, e.g. frog

cards.term: Site of gas exchange in an insect?
cards.definition: The fine ends of the tracheal tubes (tracheoles), in direct contact with tissues

cards.term: Path of air from nostrils to lungs?
cards.definition: External nostrils → nasal passage → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli

cards.term: What is the common passage for food and air?
cards.definition: Part of the pharynx

cards.term: Why is the larynx called the sound box?
cards.definition: It is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production
A thin elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing, stopping food entering the larynx

cards.term: At which level does the trachea divide into primary bronchi?
cards.definition: The 5th thoracic vertebra

cards.term: Which airways have incomplete cartilaginous rings?
cards.definition: Trachea, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles

cards.term: Why are the cartilage rings incomplete (C-shaped)?
cards.definition: They keep the airway open while the open back lets the oesophagus expand during swallowing (intuition)
Very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures at the end of terminal bronchioles
A double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between the layers
Reduces friction on the lung surface
Outer: in contact with the thoracic lining. Inner: in contact with the lung surface.
Conducting: external nostrils to terminal bronchioles. Exchange: alveoli and their ducts.
Transports air to alveoli, clears foreign particles, humidifies, brings air to body temperature

cards.term: Why does gas exchange happen only in alveoli?
cards.definition: Only alveoli have very thin walls in close contact with a dense capillary network
Dorsally: vertebral column. Ventrally: sternum. Laterally: ribs. Below: dome-shaped diaphragm.

cards.term: Why must the thoracic chamber be air-tight?
cards.definition: Any change in thoracic volume is reflected in the lung volume; we cannot change lung volume directly

cards.text: Steps of respiration: (i) {{c1::breathing (pulmonary ventilation)}} → (ii) diffusion across the {{c2::alveolar membrane}} → (iii) {{c3::transport by blood}} → (iv) diffusion between blood and {{c4::tissues}} → (v) {{c5::cellular respiration}}.

cards.definition: Inspiration (air drawn in) and expiration (alveolar air released)
When intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (negative pressure)
When intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure

cards.term: Which muscles create the pressure gradients?
cards.definition: The diaphragm and external and internal intercostals

cards.term: What does contraction of the diaphragm do?
cards.definition: Increases thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis

cards.term: What does contraction of external intercostals do?
cards.definition: Lifts ribs and sternum: increases thoracic volume in the dorso-ventral axis
Diaphragm and external intercostals contract → thoracic and pulmonary volume ↑ → intra-pulmonary pressure ↓ below atmospheric → air rushes in
Diaphragm and intercostals relax → thoracic volume ↓ → pressure rises slightly above atmospheric → air is expelled

cards.term: Is normal expiration active or passive?
cards.definition: Passive (muscle relaxation). Forceful breathing uses abdominal muscles.

cards.term: Which muscles increase the strength of breathing?
cards.definition: Additional muscles in the abdomen

cards.term: Normal breathing rate of a healthy human?
cards.definition: 12–16 times per minute
Spirometer
Air inspired or expired in a normal breath: about 500 mL

cards.term: Air breathed per minute by a healthy man?
cards.definition: 6000–8000 mL (TV × 12–16)

cards.term: Tidal volume of a healthy human in an hour (approx.)?
cards.definition: ≈ 360–480 L (6–8 L/min × 60)
Extra air inspired by forcible inspiration: 2500–3000 mL
Extra air expired by forcible expiration: 1000–1100 mL
Air remaining in lungs even after forcible expiration: 1100–1200 mL

cards.text: Inspiratory capacity (IC) = {{c1::TV + IRV}}. Expiratory capacity (EC) = {{c2::TV + ERV}}.
Functional residual capacity (FRC) = {{c1::ERV + RV}}: air left after a normal expiration.
Vital capacity (VC) = {{c1::ERV + TV + IRV}}. Total lung capacity (TLC) = {{c2::VC + RV}}.

cards.definition: Maximum air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or out after a forced inspiration)
It indicates lung fitness: higher in athletes, mountain dwellers, swimmers, lower in smokers and lung disease

cards.term: Volume of air in the lungs after a normal expiration?
cards.definition: FRC = ERV + RV ≈ 2100–2300 mL

cards.term: Which volume cannot be measured by a spirometer?
cards.definition: Residual volume (and so FRC and TLC). It never leaves the lungs.
Volumes are single blocks (TV, IRV, ERV, RV). Capacities = sum of 2+ volumes. Any capacity with "residual" or "total" includes RV.

cards.definition: Alveoli; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues

cards.term: How are O₂ and CO₂ exchanged?
cards.definition: By simple diffusion, based on pressure/concentration gradient
Partial pressure gradient, solubility of the gas, thickness of membranes
Pressure contributed by one gas in a mixture: pO₂, pCO₂
Atmospheric air: 159 / 0.3; Alveoli: 104 / 40; Deoxygenated blood: 40 / 45; Oxygenated blood: 95 / 40; Tissues: 40 / 45

cards.term: Atmospheric air vs alveolar air: pO₂ and pCO₂?
cards.definition: Atmospheric air has higher pO₂ and lower pCO₂

cards.term: Why is alveolar pO₂ (104) lower than atmospheric (159)?
cards.definition: Fresh air mixes with the residual air in the lungs, which is poorer in O₂ (and water vapour adds pressure)

cards.term: How much more soluble is CO₂ than O₂?
cards.definition: 20–25 times

cards.term: Why does CO₂ diffuse well despite a small gradient (45 → 40)?
cards.definition: Its solubility is 20–25 times that of O₂

cards.term: Three layers of the diffusion membrane?
cards.definition: Thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and the basement substance between them

cards.term: Total thickness of the diffusion membrane?
cards.definition: Much less than a millimetre

cards.term: Figure 14.3: summarise exchange at alveolus and tissues.
cards.definition: At alveoli O₂ enters blood (pO₂ 104 → 95) and CO₂ leaves (45 → 40); at tissues O₂ leaves blood and CO₂ enters
97% by RBCs; 3% dissolved in plasma
20–25% by RBCs (carbamino-haemoglobin); 70% as bicarbonate; 7% dissolved in plasma
A red, iron-containing pigment in RBCs
Four

cards.term: Main factor in O₂ binding to haemoglobin?
cards.definition: Partial pressure of O₂; pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature also interfere

cards.term: What is the oxygen dissociation curve?
cards.definition: Percentage saturation of haemoglobin with O₂ plotted against pO₂; it is sigmoid

cards.term: Why is the oxygen dissociation curve sigmoid?
cards.definition: Binding of one O₂ makes the next bind more easily (cooperative binding), so saturation rises steeply in the middle range

cards.term: Conditions in alveoli favouring oxyhaemoglobin formation?
cards.definition: High pO₂, low pCO₂, fewer H⁺, lower temperature

cards.term: Conditions in tissues favouring O₂ release?
cards.definition: Low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺, higher temperature

cards.term: Effect of pCO₂ on oxygen transport?
cards.definition: High pCO₂ (and H⁺) lowers haemoglobin's O₂ affinity: curve shifts right, O₂ released to tissues (Bohr effect)

cards.term: Mnemonic for a right shift of the O₂ curve?
cards.definition: "CADET, face Right": CO₂, Acid (H⁺), 2,3-DPG, Exercise, Temperature ↑ → curve shifts right, O₂ unloaded

cards.term: O₂ delivered to tissues per 100 mL oxygenated blood?
cards.definition: About 5 mL
CO₂ carried bound to haemoglobin (20–25% of CO₂)

cards.term: When does CO₂ bind to Hb and when is it released?
cards.definition: Binds at tissues (high pCO₂, low pO₂); released at alveoli (low pCO₂, high pO₂)

cards.term: Which enzyme helps carry CO₂ as bicarbonate, and where is it?
cards.definition: Carbonic anhydrase: very high in RBCs, minute amounts in plasma
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺

cards.term: Direction of the carbonic anhydrase reaction at tissues vs alveoli?
cards.definition: Tissues (high pCO₂): → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. Alveoli (low pCO₂): ← CO₂ + H₂O.

cards.term: CO₂ delivered to alveoli per 100 mL deoxygenated blood?
cards.definition: About 4 mL
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200× more strongly than O₂ (carboxyhaemoglobin), so O₂ transport stops
The neural system

cards.term: Where is the respiratory rhythm centre?
cards.definition: In the medulla of the brain

cards.term: Where is the pneumotaxic centre, and what does it do?
cards.definition: In the pons; it moderates the rhythm centre and can reduce the duration of inspiration, altering the rate

cards.term: What is the chemosensitive area sensitive to?
cards.definition: CO₂ and H⁺; located next to the rhythm centre

cards.term: Which peripheral receptors detect CO₂ and H⁺?
cards.definition: Receptors on the aortic arch and carotid artery

cards.term: Role of O₂ in regulating respiratory rhythm?
cards.definition: Quite insignificant. CO₂ and H⁺ are the main drivers.

cards.term: What happens to breathing on going up a hill?
cards.definition: Low pO₂ at altitude → breathing rate and depth increase; over days the body makes more RBCs (acclimatisation)
Shortage of O₂ reaching tissues, e.g. at high altitude
Difficulty in breathing with wheezing, due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles
A chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, reducing respiratory surface
Cigarette smoking
Long exposure to dust (grinding, stone-breaking) causes inflammation and fibrosis of the lungs
Proliferation of fibrous tissue, causing serious lung damage
Workers should wear protective masks
Asthma: Inflamed bronchi/bronchioles, wheezing; Emphysema: Alveolar walls damaged; Occupational disorders: Dust → inflammation → fibrosis
